source: Assessing Cognitive Biases in LLMs for Judicial Decision Support: Virtuous Victim and Halo Effects (IEEE ICDM 2025)
finding: Five LLMs were tested on sentencing-style vignettes for the virtuous victim effect and prestige (halo) effects. Models showed the human-like effects, some weaker, some stronger than humans.
numbers: Models: ChatGPT 5 Instant, ChatGPT 5 Thinking, DeepSeek V3.1, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash. 10 valid runs per prompt. Corporate prestige award ratio: 1.98x, 1.57x, 2.11x, 2.02x, 3.02x (Gemini) vs human 3.00x.
limits: Small custom vignette set (about 9 vignettes); no p-values; paper has internal number inconsistencies; no mitigation tested.
agent_relevance: Prestige of a party moves LLM awards like it moves human ones. A guardrail must strip party prestige and victim character cues before judging.

source: Same paper: virtuous victim effect, minor harm
finding: On a 9-point moral-character scale, every model rated a victim more favorably than a non-victim baseline, and most exceeded the human size.
numbers: Shift in points: Instant +0.9, Thinking +1.4, DeepSeek +0.5, Claude +0.7, Gemini +1.9; human benchmark +0.5.
limits: Human benchmark taken from earlier literature, not a matched sample.
agent_relevance: Most models over-react to victim framing versus humans. Test for this effect when the agent judges people or disputes.

source: Same paper: adjacent consent and occupational/credential prestige
finding: No model penalised victims for prior consent. Prestige effects on sentence length were mixed across models.
numbers: Occupational prestige sentence diff: Instant +0.17 yr, Thinking -0.05, DeepSeek +1.07, Gemini -0.27; human about +0.67 yr. Death-sentence likelihood (1-10) credential effect: +0.3, +0.6, +0.4, +0.1 vs human +1.5.
quote: None of the models penalized victims for giving prior consent
limits: Claude cells N/A (refusals or non-numeric). Not significance tested.
agent_relevance: Effects are model-specific and unstable; do not assume one model's profile applies to another.

source: Hu et al. (2025) LLMs on Trial: Evaluating Judicial Fairness for Large Language Models (JudiFair)
finding: Large benchmark for inconsistency, bias and imbalanced inaccuracy of LLMs on judicial tasks. Found all three to be widespread.
numbers: 16 LLMs; 65 labels, 161 label values; 177,100 unique case facts built from 1,100 judicial documents (LEEC: 15,919 documents). At temperature 0, 14 of 15 models showed significant bias and significant imbalanced inaccuracy (p<0.01).
limits: Paper has count inconsistencies (15 vs 16 models; 96 vs 161 label values). Sentence units unclear. Only first 100k of 240k characters read.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that same-case LLM judgments depend on irrelevant factors. A code-run perturbation check (swap irrelevant facts, compare) is justified.

source: Same paper: inconsistency level
finding: Even at temperature 0, LLM outputs on the same case differ across runs and framings. Higher temperature raises inconsistency.
numbers: Average inconsistency about 15-18% at temperature 0 (the text gives both). Bias-significant label values fall as temperature rises (p<0.01) because randomness masks bias.
limits: Authors use 12 random models for the temperature test.
agent_relevance: Noise and bias are separate: more sampling noise can hide bias, so measure both. Majority vote lowers noise but not bias (G4).

source: Same paper: bias drivers and model scale
finding: Demographic labels cause more bias than non-demographic ones. Bigger or newer models were not fairer.
numbers: defendant_wealth significant in 10 of 13 models; victim_age in 1. Parameter size does not reduce bias and may raise inconsistency; release date has no significant effect. Weighted MAPE of sentences vs real about 219%; mean weighted MAE 64.9 (unit unclear).
limits: Higher accuracy was correlated with higher bias (Pearson), so accuracy is not a safe proxy for fairness.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a stronger model to be less biased. Add explicit checks instead of relying on scale.

source: Tapwal, Kumar, Maple (2026) Faithful or Fabricated? Rationalization bias in LLM judges
finding: Judges shift verdicts toward a presented label (anchoring), even a placebo label, and rewrite explanations to fit it. A Proof-Before-Preference protocol (lock evidence first, then score) nearly removed this.
numbers: 1,000 summaries; 5 judges (Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen, Zephyr). Label Anchoring in Outcomes LAO = 1.00 for Baseline on true labels in all models; SCoT 0.91-1.00; PBP near 0. Placebo labels: Baseline LAO up to 1.00; SCoT 0.68-1.00; PBP 0.50-0.63 in some, near 0 in others.
limits: Small open models; summarisation task, not legal. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Strong match to G2/G3: evidence is written and locked before any score, and cues are withheld. Plain structured chain-of-thought made anchoring worse, not better.

source: Same paper: verbosity and confidence attacks, label-revision rates
finding: Padding one candidate with fluent tokens or confident wording moves outcomes. PBP held best, SCoT worst.
numbers: Verbosity attack LAO: PBP 0.00-0.18; Baseline 0.35-0.70; SCoT 0.90-0.97. Cue-aligned explanations: PBP 15-26%, Baseline 30-55%. Label-aligned revision rates: Baseline {85,78,76,83,82}%, SCoT {80,80,76,82,80}%, PBP {22,5,8,18,15}%.
limits: Same limits as above; PBP abstains more often (modest cost).
agent_relevance: Criterion-by-criterion reasoning without locked evidence can amplify anchoring (rubric-amplified rationalisation). Order the steps: evidence, lock, then verdict.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLM with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring is common in LLMs, acts in shallow layers, and cannot be removed by usual prompts. Reasoning models were least affected.
numbers: Share of questions anchored: 22% to 61% across models. Total ratio: Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Mistral-7B 51.1%, Llama-3.1-8B 34.7%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%. Human A-Index 0.4-0.6; most LLMs equal or worse.
limits: Synthetic questions, not legal. Mitigation tested only on two 7-8B models.
agent_relevance: Anchors from a prior claim or number (e.g. prosecutor demand) will pull the agent. Reasoning mode helps but does not cure; the anchor must be kept out of the prompt where possible.

source: Same paper: mitigation tests
finding: Common fixes gave small or no gains. Anti-DP (state your own standard first, then answer) helped most.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B total anchored 34.7%: question-aware prompt 36.8%, knowledge enhancement 50.5% (worse), self-improving 38.4%, adversarial LoRA 33.3%, Anti-DP 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B 40.0%: self-improving 48.0% (worse), Anti-DP 40.8%. Best gain about 10 points.
limits: Two small models; Anti-DP did not help Qwen numerical items.
agent_relevance: Do not add a generic 'be careful' or self-revision step. Fixing the standard before seeing the anchor (a pre-commit step) is the better bet.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Tested prompt-induced, sequential (anchoring, primacy) and inherent biases in student-admission decisions. Self-help debiasing worked best.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Llama-2 7B and 13B. GPT-4 admits 40.5% more students under reject framing. Llama-2 7B classes 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Models prefer first options A/B (primacy).
limits: Admissions, not courts; older models. Few-shot and counterfactual prompts often broke instruction following (probability driven to 0 or 1).
agent_relevance: Order effects are real in option lists: shuffle option order in code and compare. Let the model rewrite the prompt to remove bias cues only if it is a large model.

source: Same paper: anchoring and self-help results
finding: When allowed to revise after seeing all items at once, small models changed many decisions; high-capacity models removed bias cues from prompts better.
numbers: Change rates after self-help: GPT-3.5 0.052, GPT-4 0.175, Llama-2-13b 0.521, Llama-2-7b 0.399. Self-help reduced biased prompt parts to 0 for group attribution and 2.7% for framing in GPT-4.
limits: Change rate shows inconsistency but not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Revision only from real output (G2): self-help works as a rewrite of the prompt, not as an opinion about the answer.

source: Kumar, Rathore, Moitra (2026) All Verdicts are Not Equal: Rethinking LLM Judge Reliability
finding: Audit of LLM judges split verdict instability into run-to-run noise and order (position) bias. Order swaps flip many verdicts; determinism does not mean accuracy.
numbers: 6 models, 4 benchmarks, 5 formats, 2 orders, 3 temperatures, 10 repeats. 7-17% of verdicts change across identical replications; up to 98% flip when order is swapped. One judge repeated the same verdict 100% of the time with 51% accuracy.
limits: Pairwise evaluation tasks, not legal; vendor audit paper.
agent_relevance: Run each comparison in both orders in code and treat disagreement as no verdict. Never take repeat-agreement as proof.

source: Same paper: accuracy ceiling from position bias and format effects
finding: Position flip rate sets a hard ceiling on accuracy. Output format change alone moved trustworthiness a lot.
numbers: Ceiling A <= 1 - flip/2. Gemini-2.5-Pro on JudgeBench: Direct prompt A 63.5%, T 28.9%; Verdict-first JSON A 88.5%, T 77.5%, position flips 56.0% to 6.9%. Temperature reduces consistency by 12.1 points.
limits: Reliability is item-specific; a single judge-format result is not a stable estimate.
agent_relevance: A format choice can matter as much as the model. Fix the output format and test it for order flips before use.

source: Same paper: rubric scoring
finding: Holistic rubric scoring (G-Eval) improved trustworthiness more than any single prompt format change; FLASK decomposition collapsed for five of six judges (as stated in abstract and section 5.6).
numbers: Three paradigms compared on JudgeBench and LLMBar at temperature 0 (Table 2). Exact per-judge gains not extracted.
limits: Per-cell numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Scoring each option on a scale avoids the first-position effect of pairwise choice.

source: Ayal, Elyoseph, Solomon (2026) Evaluating Large Language Models as Judicial Decision-Makers, Justice Quarterly 43(5)
finding: LLMs gave much less spread in sentences than 123 retired judges on two fictional cases (rape, violence). Each LLM was closer to the judges' mean than judges were individually.
numbers: 123 retired judges; 2 cases; GPT, Gemini, Claude; zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought.
quote: LLMs showed greater consistency, producing significantly lower sentence disparity than judges.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. The judges' mean is a convenience benchmark, not truth. Low spread may hide shared bias.
agent_relevance: Low noise is easy to get; bias stays (see JudiFair). Use LLMs for noise reduction only with bias checks.

source: Zambrano (2025) The Judge Variable: Challenging Judge-Agnostic Legal Judgment Prediction
finding: Hybrid LLM feature extraction plus ML predicted French custody rulings better with per-judge models than a pooled model, so judge identity carries a stable signal (system noise).
numbers: 18,937 rulings from 10,306 cases. Specialist (per-judge) F1 up to 92.85% vs generalist 82.63% trained on 20x to 100x more data.
limits: Judge-specific patterns do not transfer across judges; one domain, one country.
agent_relevance: Shows level/pattern noise can be learned. An agent should not imitate one judge's pattern as if it were the law.

source: Zhang and Xu (2025) The Consistency-Acceptability Divergence of LLMs in Judicial Decision-Making
finding: Policy review: high LLM consistency is not the same as legitimacy; value-heavy tasks lose acceptance.
numbers: Compiles 2023-2025 reports; cites a Shenzhen court rollout and a survey of 1,000 adults.
limits: Secondary, uses reports of other studies; not primary evidence.
agent_relevance: Low value as evidence; useful for framing only.

source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Extraneous factors in judicial decisions (as summarised in search results)
finding: Original hungry-judge claim: favourable rulings fell from about 65% to near zero before a break and rebounded after.
numbers: 1,112 parole decisions, 8 judges, 50 days, 10 months, Israel.
limits: Critics say case order and scheduling explain it (Glockner). Only search snippets seen.
agent_relevance: Do not build an agent fatigue rule from this; the effect is probably an artefact. LLMs have no hunger, but context length can act like fatigue and should be tested directly.

source: Chatziathanasiou (2022) Beware the lure of narratives: hungry judges should not motivate AI in law, German Law Journal
finding: Argues the hungry-judge study cannot support the case for AI in law.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Do not cite hungry judges as motivation for LLM judging.

source: Gap: no LLM test of time-of-day, hunger or session-order effects found
finding: Searches for LLM replications of the Danziger result found none. Order-in-session effects in LLMs are untested in the sources found.
numbers: 0 studies found.
limits: Absence in a limited search (search budget ran out), not proof.
agent_relevance: Open gap. Cheap test: run the same case at position 1 vs 200 in a long context and compare outcomes.

source: Apart Research hackathon submission (2025) noise audit of repeated LLM legal judgments
finding: Reported two LLMs near chance accuracy on legal cases with low or no variance across repeated runs.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not seen.
limits: Hackathon write-up, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Reinforces: low noise with chance accuracy, as in the verdict audit.

source: National Law Review (2025) Same question, different answers: what 12,000 tests reveal about AI and legal
finding: Practitioner article on repeated tests: very similar cases can be decided differently by an LLM.
numbers: About 12,000 tests, per title; details not read.
limits: Trade press, snippet only.
agent_relevance: Supports running multiple perturbed copies of a case.

source: Englich and Mussweiler (2001) sentencing anchors (cited in the 2026 LLM paper related work)
finding: Human judges are anchored by a prosecutor demand. The 2026 LLM papers cite it as the human baseline; no LLM replication of the sentencing-demand paradigm was found.
numbers: Human numbers not read here.
limits: Cited via related-work in an LLM paper.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the Englich paradigm is a clear gap; cheap to run.

source: Journal of Law and Analytics (2025) bias from human-AI interaction among 139 Chinese judges
finding: Study of 139 Chinese judges on bias created in human-AI interaction. Authors say results are suggestive, not definitive (not pre-registered).
numbers: N=139 judges.
limits: Only the search snippet was seen.
agent_relevance: Judges can be anchored by AI output; an agent's own draft may anchor its later steps (G4).
